extracted.intended_audience: Science News readers, news sources, Science News staff and freelance science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Organization-specific editorial policies and standards used by Science News for reporting, editing, fact-checking, sourcing, visuals, corrections and the use of AI in science journalism. Intended to guide reporters, editors, freelancers and inform readers about newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: We write about science, medicine and technology broadly, including new findings and techniques, surprising statistics and the latest science trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers new findings and techniques, surprising statistics and trends; reporters may explain science related to current events and monitor developments in a field to spot trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer qualifications and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of our writers specialize in a particular area of science. Our staff combines experience in scientific research — many writers have Ph.D.s or other degrees in areas related to the topics they write about — and in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may be staff or freelancers; experience in research and journalism helps gather, critically assess and present information; bios of writers are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of story ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Story ideas can come from anywhere, including reading studies in scientific journals, attending scientific conferences, exploring science behind topics of reader interest, scanning the news, talking with scientists/policymakers/public and monitoring field developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common methods listed: reading major journals (Science, Nature, field journals), conferences, public interest topics, news scanning, expert recommendations and trend monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating quality of a published study
rubrics_metrics.description: We evaluate the size of a study, including the number of participants or the amount of data collected, and assess whether the data presented match the researchers’ interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically consult outside experts not involved in the research; gauge whether statistical significance has real-world relevance; in some cases verify analyses with statisticians; interview scientists whose work is referenced; consider how many lines of evidence support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of non–peer-reviewed research (preprints, conference findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we cover research that hasn’t been peer-reviewed — such as findings at a conference or a paper on a preprint server — we approach it with extra care and might consult more outside experts than we otherwise would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask researchers what feedback they've received and how much is likely to change in peer review; gauge how far from publication a finding is and major remaining questions; sometimes avoid writing about overly preliminary work, other times report if implications are striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cautious/qualifying language
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and editors use terms such as 'suggests' or 'could' when a finding is not yet certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms reflect caveats, limitations and alternate explanations and are used to place findings in context; rarely does one study fully answer a question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of press embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes forbid publishing a story about a given topic until a certain time and explain why many outlets publish simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargoed materials give reporters time to prepare accurate stories; institutions often send releases or papers to journalists a few days in advance under embargo to encourage coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who to interview / range of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers look broadly for sources including authors of papers, experts cited in a paper, trusted contacts, recommendations from other experts, policy makers, patients, industry leaders and people affected by developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-scientist voices are used to capture perspectives of those affected and to provide policy or societal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of outside experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing outside experts who weren’t involved in the research can provide an independent assessment and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside experts can put a study into context, assess importance, and point out strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating source credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers try to find subject-matter experts who can provide accurate and up-to-date information and check sources’ institutional affiliations, publications and sometimes social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask sources about personal biases or financial conflicts and generally avoid sources who might have conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial review for short news vs features
rubrics_metrics.description: For shorter news stories, at least one content editor sees a story before publication. For longer features, the first draft is reviewed by multiple editors as well as design and web production teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors ensure news and context are clear and important details are included and accurate; longer pieces can take weeks to months in editing; design/web teams plan images and media concurrently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of design and web teams in production
rubrics_metrics.description: Design director and assistant art directors choose and edit photos, videos and infographics or create those visuals. Web production and social media craft headlines, post stories online and create social posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams coordinate to plan images and other media early in the feature editing process; social/web teams optimize presentation and promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection, accuracy and licensing of visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Design team researches visual options and checks to make sure they are accurate and that we have complied with all licensing requirements, including crediting the source of the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design may commission original illustrations, graphics, photography and video or create visuals in-house; visuals should accurately convey scientific concepts and be properly credited/licensed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking coverage (which pieces get fact-checked)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to time constraints, news stories published online do not regularly go through a distinct fact-checking process. Feature stories are fact-checked before they are posted online, and online stories that later appear in print are fact-checked before print publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors perform fact-checking duties for online stories such as checking names, affiliations and numbers and looking for logical inconsistencies; writers also check their facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking process and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Science News has two staff members who fact-check content, and we also rely on freelance fact-checkers. Fact-checkers confirm the accuracy of all parts of a story, including headlines, photo captions and credits, data in graphs or charts and the raw data behind visualizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-checkers use materials provided by the writer (papers, websites, notes/transcripts) and perform independent research; they do not call sources to check the quotes used in a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source review policy prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s the responsibility of writers to ensure the accuracy of quotes. Writers often return to a source to check facts, but sources are not allowed to review articles prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice preserves editorial independence and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and updating policy
rubrics_metrics.description: We publish corrections for factual errors as well as any misleading or mischaracterizing statements. When an online story is updated, an editor’s note at the end of the story indicates what text has been fixed, why, and the date of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For print stories, corrections typically appear on the Feedback page of the earliest print issue after the error is identified; editors and writers determine how to correct errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence is the freedom of editors and writers to report and write topics at will, without an external party’s involvement. No institution, government body, scientist or other entity, including our publisher, the Society for Science, determines what we write about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science News publishes stories only on what it finds newsworthy; see About page for more on independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: We try to avoid conflicts of interest whenever possible. However, when such conflicts are unavoidable, we disclose them to our readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when covering work of a scientist who has a relationship with the parent organization (e.g., Board of Trustees member), we disclose that relationship in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to controversial topics and scientific consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: We focus on data and facts, and we note limitations or caveats in research findings. Science News doesn’t present 'both sides' of an issue when there is a clear scientific consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label opinion/commentary clearly; report well-established science even if popular opinion disagrees (examples: age of Earth, evolution, vaccines, human-caused climate change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding transparency and editorial independence from supporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Science News is published by the Society for Science, a nonprofit. We get financial support through subscriptions, advertisements, donations, grants and sponsorships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial supporters have no influence on what is written and no knowledge of the specific content of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI prohibition for published content
rubrics_metrics.description: Science News Media Group will not publish text, images, audio or video created by AI content generators on our website, social media channels or in our print magazines — except when such content is being used as an example to show what AI does or doesn’t do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When AI-generated content is used as an example (e.g., in reporting on AI), the organization will clearly explain how the technology and its content was used and point out any errors or ethical concerns introduced through that use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted AI-assisted editing techniques for visuals and audio
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic editing techniques that sometimes rely on AI may be used so long as they don’t alter the substance, change the meaning of the original content or mislead the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include removing lines/labels/scale bars, using Photoshop Content-Aware Fill to expand backgrounds, and using noise reduction tools in audio; be transparent about whether visuals are photographs, composites or illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI tools for workflows and audio production with oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Science News uses an AI-generated voice to produce audio versions of articles online and is exploring AI for brainstorming, workflows and social promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audio versions produced with AI voice are regularly reviewed for accuracy; the organization will be transparent about how AI tools are used and update the policy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to human-generated content and remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: We are steadfast in our commitment to publishing original, human-generated content that meets our standards of accuracy and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If published content does not align with policy regarding AI or other standards, Science News will correct the problem and clearly disclose the error to the audience (correction, editor’s note, or removal with note).
